source_caption:
The famous blue door that served as the entrance to William Thacker’s flat wasn’t a studio set piece—it was the actual front door of screenwriter Richard Curtis’s former house in the real Notting Hill neighborhood. After the film became a massive global hit, the flat became such an overwhelming tourist attraction that fans would constantly knock on it and take photos at all hours of the day and night. The new owners of the property became so deeply frustrated by the endless stream of visitors that they painted the door black to try and disguise it from movie fans. Eventually, the original blue door was removed from the frame entirely and successfully auctioned off at Christie’s to raise money for charity, though a replacement blue door was later installed to appease tourists.

Notting Hill (1999), directed by Roger Michell, starring Julia Roberts, Hugh Grant, Rhys Ifans, Emma Chambers. A humble, mild-mannered London bookstore owner finds his quiet, predictable life completely turned upside down when the world’s most famous and glamorous American movie star wanders into his shop, sparking an unlikely, highly publicized romance.

source_details.title: Notting Hill
source_details.synopsis: Notting Hill is a 1999 romantic comedy film directed by Roger Michell, written by Richard Curtis, and produced by Duncan Kenworthy. It stars Julia Roberts and Hugh Grant, with Rhys Ifans, Emma Chambers, Tim McInnerny, Gina McKee, and Hugh Bonneville in supporting roles. The story is of a romance between a British bookshop keeper (Grant) and a famous American actress (Roberts) who happens to walk into his shop in London's Notting Hill district. Released on 21 May 1999 in the United Kingdom by PolyGram Filmed Entertainment and on 28 May 1999 in the United States by Universal Pictures, Notting Hill was well received by critics and was the highest-grossing British film of all time upon release,
